procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Additional Senior Sub-Judge, Hoshiarpur
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Superintendent of Police, Hoshiarpur dated 9.9.1980 discharging the appellant from service under Rule 12.21 volume 7 of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A Regular Second Appeal No. 2198 of 1984 was filed before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh. The said Second Appeal was dismissed on 10.10.1984.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant filed a special leave petition to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution after the High Court dismissed her appeal. Special Leave was granted and arguments were heard. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: A writ of certiorari be issued on the respondents to quash and set aside the impugned order dated 9.9.1980 of her dismissal from service.
A writ in the nature of mandamus and appropriate directions be issued to allow the appellant to be reinstated in the post from which she has been discharged.

The authorities concerned will pay all her emoluments to which she is entitled to in accordance with the extant rules as early as possible in any case not later than eight weeks from the date of this judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the termination of a temporary or probationary employee, ostensibly under service rules, can be considered a punitive measure amounting to removal from service under Article 311(2) of the Constitution if it is based on allegations of misconduct without a proper inquiry.

facts: The appellant was a temporary lady constable.
She was discharged from service by an order that stated she was 'unlikely to prove an efficient police officer', ostensibly under Rule 12.21 of the Punjab Police Rules.
This order was issued following an investigation into allegations of misconduct against her, which was conducted behind her back.
The appellant was not served a chargesheet, asked for an explanation, or given any opportunity to show cause or cross-examine witnesses before her termination.
law: Article 311(2) of the Constitution requires that a civil servant be given a reasonable opportunity to show cause before being dismissed or removed from service as a punitive measure.
The court can look beyond the form of a termination order to ascertain its true character. An order that appears innocuous can be a 'camouflage' or a 'cloak' for a punitive dismissal.

If the termination of a temporary or probationary employee is founded on misconduct, negligence, or inefficiency, it is considered a punishment, and the procedural requirements of Article 311 must be complied with.
Discharging a probationer for misconduct without a proper inquiry and an opportunity to be heard can amount to removal from service under Article 311(2).
application: The Court looked behind the innocuous wording of the discharge order, which cited inefficiency under service rules.
It found that the 'irresistible conclusion' was that the order was not a simple termination but was based on a finding of misconduct from an inquiry held behind the appellant's back.
The Court determined that the order was, in reality, a 'camouflage for an order of dismissal from service on the ground of misconduct.'
Because the termination was punitive and based on misconduct, it cast a 'stigma' on the appellant's service career.
The failure to provide a chargesheet, seek an explanation, or offer an opportunity to be heard was a 'total contravention' of the protections guaranteed by Article 311(2).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that even though the termination order was framed in innocuous terms under service rules, it was in substance a punitive dismissal for misconduct. Since the termination was based on allegations of misconduct without affording the employee the procedural safeguards of a proper inquiry as required by Article 311(2) of the Constitution, the order was unconstitutional and liable to be quashed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the termination of a temporary or probationary employee, ostensibly under service rules, can be considered a punitive measure amounting to removal from service under Article 311(2) of the Constitution if it is based on allegations of misconduct without a proper inquiry.
appellant_arguments: The order of discharge was not a simple termination under service rules but was a punitive measure based on allegations of misconduct.
The finding of misconduct was based on an investigation conducted behind her back.
The termination order was issued without serving a chargesheet, asking for an explanation, or providing an opportunity to show cause or cross-examine witnesses.
This procedure contravenes the protections guaranteed under Article 311(2) of the Constitution, making the order liable to be quashed.
respondent_arguments: The order discharging the appellant was not punitive.

The order was made in accordance with Rule 12.21 of the Punjab Police Rules, which allows the Superintendent of Police to discharge a constable within three years of enrolment if they are found unlikely to be an efficient police officer.
Since the order was made in accordance with the appellant's conditions of service, it is unchallengeable.

cases.case_name: Shamsher Singh & Anr. v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: The termination of a probationer's services, even if the order is worded innocuously, can amount to a punitive removal from service under Article 311(2) if it is based on misconduct or inefficiency without a proper inquiry and a reasonable opportunity for the employee to show cause.

cases.case_name: Anoop Jaiswal v. Government of India & Anr.
cases.principle: The court can look behind a seemingly simple termination order to determine its true nature. If the order is found to be a 'camouflage' for a punitive dismissal based on misconduct, it is invalid for contravening Article 311(2) if no proper inquiry was conducted.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The form of an order terminating employment is not conclusive of its true nature, and a court may examine the surrounding circumstances to ascertain its real character. The overriding test is whether an employee's misconduct was merely the motive for the termination or the very foundation of the order. If the order is found to be a punishment for misconduct disguised as a simple termination, it is invalid.
obiter: The question of whether a temporary employee's termination order can be assailed as violative of constitutional protections has been well-settled by several decisions of this Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: On a conspectus of all these decisions mentioned hereinbefore, the irresistible conclusion follows that the impugned order of discharge though couched in innocuous terms,. is merely a camouflage for an order of dismissal from service on the ground of misconduct. This order has been made without serving the appellant any charge-sheet, without asking for any explanation from her and without giving any opportunity to show cause against the purported order of dismissal from service and without giving any opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses examined, that is, in other words the order has been made in total contravention of the provisions of Article 311(2) of the constitution.
legal_tests_applied: The form of an order is not conclusive of its true nature; it might be a cloak or camouflage for an order founded on misconduct. The entirety of the circumstances must be examined, and the overriding test is whether the misconduct is a mere motive or the very foundation of the order.

If a probationer is discharged on the ground of misconduct or inefficiency without a proper enquiry and without a reasonable opportunity of showing cause, it may amount to removal from service within the meaning of Article 311(2) of the Constitution.
policy_considerations: The court prioritizes the substance of a termination order over its form to prevent the circumvention of constitutional protections.
Even temporary or probationary employees are protected by Article 311(2) if their termination is punitive and based on misconduct, as such an order casts a stigma on their service career.

Upholding the principles of natural justice is paramount, requiring that an employee be given a fair opportunity to defend themselves against allegations of misconduct before a punitive action is taken.
